messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Chef
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Violence: Violence, Auditory (Cars): Car sounds, Loss of Control: Lack of control
  Maladaptive Strategies: Revenge Fantasies: I imagine getting revenge on the people responsible, Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury, Memory Detachment: I detach myself from the memories
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
  Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening, Hopelessness: I have no future

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame is a 21-year-old single man who emigrated to the United States from Africa with his family as a teenager and now works long hours as a chef in a busy restaurant kitchen. He described the assault with effort and visible strain, repeatedly losing his place when he tried to tell it in order. What emerged over several sessions was that one night after work, when he was exhausted and alone, he was sexually assaulted by men he understood to be capable of serious violence. What remains most vivid to him is not a clean sequence of images but a sensory impression of being overpowered and unable to control what was happening. He remembers the soundscape with unusual sharpness: the traffic outside, a car passing, the abrupt noises around him during the assault. Even now, when the memory breaks through, it often comes with sounds in his head before anything else, as if he is hearing the event again rather than merely thinking about it.

In the days afterward, Kwame did not feel able to make sense of what had happened in words. When people asked if he was okay, he said he was tired. Inside, he had come to believe that what hurt most was not only that he had been assaulted, but that he had behaved in ways that felt completely at odds with the kind of man he believed himself to be. He was harsh with himself, certain that somebody else would have stopped it, fought harder, taken control somehow. He returned again and again to the idea that he had failed a test that another person would have passed. When he tried to explain this, he would stop mid-sentence, stare at the floor, and say that the story disappears when he reaches certain parts, as if his mind cuts out.

Over the following months, the world became difficult to trust. In the restaurant kitchen, sudden movements from coworkers made him flinch and square his shoulders before he had time to think. A server brushing past quickly behind him or another chef turning with a hot pan could put him instantly on guard. The kitchen was already loud, full of clatter and sharp calls, but the sounds that unsettled him most were from outside: engines revving, cars passing the alley by the back entrance, doors slamming in the street. At those moments, the memory could return without warning, complete and immediate, leaving him feeling as if he were back in that night rather than standing at his station. He found these episodes especially frightening because they seemed to come out of nowhere. Nothing had to be obviously dangerous; sometimes his body reacted first, his heart surging and muscles tightening, while another part of him knew he was at work and nothing was actually happening.

He began watching his body constantly for signs that something was wrong. He checked for pain, tension, injuries, any sensation that might mean he was vulnerable again. Even at home in his apartment, with the door locked, he did not feel settled. He stayed alert to noises in the building and to the possibility that someone could enter, and he noticed himself reacting to ordinary sounds as if they were warnings. He did not experience home as a place where he could fully stand down.

Kwame also described the private mental habits that had grown around the assault. At times he pushed the memory away so forcefully that he felt detached from it, almost as if it had happened to someone else. At other times he was consumed by fantasies of revenge against the people responsible. He did not present these as plans, but as repetitive images that gave shape to his anger and humiliation. Alongside them was a bleak conviction that his future had narrowed or disappeared altogether. He spoke about upcoming years as if they belonged to other people. Work became something he endured shift by shift rather than a career he could imagine building.

What finally brought him to treatment was a recent incident during service when a coworker made a sudden movement behind him at the same moment a car backfired outside. Kwame spun around in alarm, visibly shaken, and had to leave the line. Afterward he was embarrassed and could not explain to his supervisor what had happened; once again he lost the thread when he tried. He came to therapy exhausted by living as if danger could break in anywhere, ashamed of how he judges himself for the assault, and frightened by how quickly ordinary sounds or movements can pull him back into it. At the same time, he said he was hoping for one thing very plainly: to feel that his life is not already over at 21.
